A field guide to a small cache

By MeshCache test drive

A cache is most useful when its limits are clear. This sample article exists only to exercise the local MeshCache extension. It contains no publisher content, personal information, or account identifiers. The contributor decides when to capture the page, reviews the result, and chooses whether to keep a private copy.

Keeping metadata apart from content gives the system two distinct jobs. A small directory can count signed votes, sort timestamps, and build a useful list without downloading article bodies. Readers retrieve a selected copy directly from the mesh and run their own integrity and formatting checks.

An explicit interface makes each decision visible. Opening an article does not share it. Opening the extension does not publish anything. The preview shows the captured text, and the cache buttons explain whether that copy stays on this device or is offered to other readers.

Storage should remain predictable as the collection grows. A count limit catches many tiny records, while a byte limit catches a smaller number of large ones. Expiry removes stale records, and eviction chooses older reader downloads before the contributor captures that were deliberately saved.

Observability describes what actually happened. An indexing run records the number of public metadata entries it received, how long the query took, and whether a failure prevented an update. A failed run leaves the previous directory available rather than replacing it with an incomplete result.

Popularity is a preference signal, not proof of correctness. A signature identifies a key, and a timestamp identifies a claimed capture time. Neither proves that the article is complete or authentic. The reader still checks the copy before rendering it and can compare it with the original source.

What a reader should expect

A clear choice, a readable copy, and a small local archive. No article is captured until its contributor presses a button.
